subject: science
name: Earth as a System
summary: Earth works as one connected system of five spheres — geosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, atmosphere and biosphere — powered by energy from the Sun. Uneven heating drives winds and ocean currents, and matter keeps cycling through the water, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen cycles. Human activities are disturbing these cycles, causing global warming, eutrophication and ozone depletion, and global agreements and lifestyle changes aim to fix this.

topics.title: Earth's spheres and how they interact
topics.summary: Earth has five interacting spheres: geosphere (rock), hydrosphere (liquid water), cryosphere (ice), atmosphere (air) and biosphere (life). A change in one affects the others.
topics.simple: Think of Earth as a team of five parts that are always working together: the **rocks and soil**, the **water**, the **ice**, the **air**, and all **living things**. If something happens to one part — say, forests are cut down — the air, water and soil are affected too. That's why we call Earth a **system**.
topics.explain:
A **system** is a set of connected parts that affect each other. Scientists describe Earth as five **spheres**:

- **Geosphere (lithosphere):** the solid Earth — rocks, minerals, soil, mountains and the hot interior
- **Hydrosphere:** all liquid water — oceans, rivers, lakes, groundwater, and water vapour in the air. About 97% of Earth's water is salty ocean water.
- **Cryosphere:** all frozen water — glaciers, ice sheets (Antarctica, Greenland), sea ice, snow and permafrost. Most of Earth's fresh water is stored here.
- **Atmosphere:** the layer of gases around Earth, held by gravity
- **Biosphere:** all living things and the places where they live — it overlaps the other four spheres

**The spheres interact all the time.** For example:
- A **volcano** (geosphere) throws ash and gases into the atmosphere, which can cool the climate and affect plants (biosphere).
- **Plants** (biosphere) take in carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and water from the soil, and release water vapour and oxygen.
- **Rain** (hydrosphere) weathers rocks (geosphere) and carries soil to rivers and seas.
- **Melting glaciers** (cryosphere) raise sea levels (hydrosphere) and feed rivers like the Ganga.

The whole system runs on **energy from the Sun** (and some heat from Earth's interior). Matter is not lost — it keeps being **recycled** between the spheres through cycles such as the water, carbon and nitrogen cycles.
topics.example: When heavy monsoon rain (hydrosphere) falls on a hillside where trees have been cut (biosphere), the soil (geosphere) washes away, causing landslides and muddy rivers. One change in one sphere ripples through the others.
keyPoints: Five spheres: geosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, atmosphere, biosphere
Cryosphere = all frozen water (glaciers, ice sheets, snow)
Biosphere overlaps all the other spheres
Spheres constantly interact — a change in one affects others
The system is powered mainly by the Sun; matter is recycled

topics.title: Energy from the Sun: insolation, albedo and latitude
topics.summary: Sunlight travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s. About 1.36 kW/m² (the solar constant) reaches the top of the atmosphere and about 1 kW/m² reaches the surface. Albedo is the fraction of light reflected; the equator gets more direct sunlight and is warmer than the poles.
topics.simple: Almost all of Earth's energy comes from the **Sun**. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us. Some of it is reflected straight back to space — white snow reflects a lot, dark oceans very little. This reflecting power is called **albedo**. Places near the **equator** get sunlight almost straight down, so they are hotter than the poles, where sunlight comes in at a slant.
topics.explain:
**Solar radiation** travels through space at the speed of light, **3 × 10⁸ m/s**.

**Solar constant:** the amount of solar energy reaching each square metre at the **top of the atmosphere**, facing the Sun, is about **1.36 kW/m²** (roughly 1.36–1.4 kW/m²). Because some is absorbed and scattered by the atmosphere, only about **1 kW/m²** reaches the **surface** on a clear day with the Sun high in the sky.

**Insolation** (*in*coming *sol*ar radi*ation*) is the solar energy actually received at a place. It depends on latitude, season, time of day and cloud cover.

**Albedo** = fraction of incoming sunlight that a surface **reflects** (from 0 = reflects nothing to 1 = reflects everything).
- **Fresh snow:** about **0.8–0.9** (reflects most light)
- **Ocean water:** about **0.06–0.1** (absorbs most light)
- Earth's overall average is about 0.3

This matters: when ice melts, darker water or land is exposed, which absorbs more heat, which melts more ice — a **feedback** that speeds up warming.

**Effect of latitude:**
- Near the **equator**, the Sun's rays fall almost **vertically** — the energy is concentrated on a small area and passes through less atmosphere, so it is **warmer**.
- Near the **poles**, rays fall at a **slant** — the same energy spreads over a larger area and passes through more atmosphere, so it is **colder**.

This **uneven heating** of Earth is what drives winds and ocean currents.
topics.deep: Why ~8 minutes? The Sun is about 1.5 × 10¹¹ m away. Time = distance ÷ speed = (1.5 × 10¹¹ m) ÷ (3 × 10⁸ m/s) = 500 s ≈ 8 minutes 20 seconds. So when you look at the Sun (never directly!), you see it as it was about 8 minutes ago.
topics.example:
Worked example: a solar panel of area 2 m² is placed in bright sunlight where about 1 kW/m² reaches the ground.

Power falling on the panel = 1 kW/m² × 2 m² = **2 kW**.

If the panel converts 20% of this to electricity: 0.20 × 2 kW = **0.4 kW (400 W)**.
keyPoints: Light travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s; takes ~8 min 20 s from the Sun
Solar constant ≈ 1.36 kW/m² at top of atmosphere; ~1 kW/m² at surface
Insolation = incoming solar radiation received at a place
Albedo = fraction reflected: fresh snow 0.8–0.9, ocean 0.06–0.1
Equator gets direct rays → warmer; poles get slanting rays → colder
Uneven heating drives winds and ocean currents

topics.title: The atmosphere: composition and layers
topics.summary: Air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon and 0.04% carbon dioxide. The atmosphere has five layers: troposphere (0–12 km, weather), stratosphere (12–50 km, ozone layer), mesosphere (50–80 km), thermosphere (80–700 km) and exosphere.
topics.simple: The air around Earth is mostly **nitrogen** (about 78%) and **oxygen** (about 21%), with tiny amounts of other gases like carbon dioxide. The atmosphere is arranged in layers. We live in the lowest layer, the **troposphere**, where all the weather happens. Above it, the **stratosphere** has the **ozone layer**, which blocks harmful UV rays from the Sun.
topics.explain:
**Composition of dry air (by volume):**
- **Nitrogen (N₂): ~78%**
- **Oxygen (O₂): ~21%**
- **Argon (Ar): ~0.9%**
- **Carbon dioxide (CO₂): ~0.04%**
- Traces of neon, helium, methane, ozone and others

Air also contains varying amounts of **water vapour** and dust. Though CO₂ and water vapour are small in amount, they are important **greenhouse gases** that keep Earth warm enough for life.

**Layers of the atmosphere** (from the ground up):
1. **Troposphere (0 to about 12 km):** contains most of the air and nearly all water vapour, so **all weather** — clouds, rain, storms — happens here. Temperature **falls** as you go up.
2. **Stratosphere (about 12 to 50 km):** contains the **ozone layer**, which absorbs harmful **ultraviolet (UV)** radiation. Because of this absorption, temperature **rises** with height here. The air is calm, so long-distance jet planes often cruise near its base.
3. **Mesosphere (about 50 to 80 km):** the **coldest** layer; most **meteors** burn up here, making 'shooting stars'.
4. **Thermosphere (about 80 to 700 km):** very thin air, but it absorbs high-energy solar radiation and gets extremely hot. **Auroras** occur here, and the International Space Station orbits in this layer. It includes the **ionosphere**, which reflects some radio waves.
5. **Exosphere (above about 700 km):** the outermost, extremely thin layer that gradually merges into space.

Air pressure and density are greatest at the surface and decrease with height — which is why mountaineers on high peaks often carry oxygen.
topics.example: A pressure cooker is needed in hill stations like Leh because air pressure is lower at high altitude, so water boils below 100 °C and food takes longer to cook in an open pot.
keyPoints: Troposphere 0–12 km: weather; temperature falls with height
Stratosphere 12–50 km: ozone layer absorbs UV
Mesosphere 50–80 km: coldest; meteors burn up
Thermosphere 80–700 km: auroras, ISS; exosphere merges into space
Air pressure and density decrease with height

topics.title: Winds, pressure belts and ocean currents
topics.summary: Wind blows from high to low pressure. Uneven heating causes sea/land and valley/mountain breezes and global pressure belts (high at ~30°, low at ~60°). The Coriolis effect deflects winds (to the right in the Northern Hemisphere). Ocean currents form gyres and move heat — the North Atlantic Drift warms Europe.
topics.simple: When air is heated, it rises and leaves behind **low pressure**; cooler air rushes in from **high pressure** areas — that moving air is **wind**. By day, land heats faster than the sea, so a cool **sea breeze** blows onto the land; at night it reverses. Because Earth spins, winds and ocean currents get bent to one side (the **Coriolis effect**). Ocean currents carry heat around the world like giant conveyor belts.
topics.explain:
**Why winds blow:** warm air expands, becomes lighter and **rises**, creating **low pressure** below. Cooler, denser air sinks, creating **high pressure**. **Wind always blows from high pressure to low pressure.**

**Local winds:**
- **Sea breeze (daytime):** land heats faster than water → low pressure over land → cool air blows **from sea to land**.
- **Land breeze (night):** land cools faster → air blows **from land to sea**.
- **Valley breeze (day):** slopes heat up → air flows **up** the valley.
- **Mountain breeze (night):** slopes cool → cold, heavy air flows **down** into the valley.

The Indian **monsoon** works on a similar idea at a much larger scale: in summer the land heats strongly and moist winds blow in from the ocean.

**Global pressure belts:**
- **Equatorial low (~0°):** hot air rises — calm, rainy region
- **Subtropical highs (~30° N and S):** air sinks — many of the world's deserts lie near here
- **Subpolar lows (~60° N and S)**
- **Polar highs (~90°)**
Winds between these belts form the planetary winds (trade winds, westerlies, polar easterlies).

**Coriolis effect:** because Earth rotates, moving air and water are **deflected** — to the **right in the Northern Hemisphere** and to the **left in the Southern Hemisphere**. The effect is zero at the equator and strongest near the poles.

**Ocean currents** are large, steady flows of ocean water, driven by **winds**, differences in **temperature and salinity** (density), **Earth's rotation** and the shape of coastlines.
- **Warm currents** move from the tropics towards the poles; **cold currents** move towards the equator.
- Large circular current systems are called **gyres** — clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere, anticlockwise in the Southern.
- The **Gulf Stream** and its extension, the **North Atlantic Drift**, carry warm water to north-west Europe, making countries like the UK and Norway much **milder** than places at the same latitude in Canada.

Winds and currents together move heat from the hot equator towards the cold poles, keeping climates more balanced.
topics.example: At a beach in Chennai or Mumbai, a cool breeze blows in from the sea in the afternoon — that's the sea breeze. Late at night, the breeze blows gently out towards the sea — the land breeze.
keyPoints: Wind blows from high pressure to low pressure
Sea breeze by day (sea → land); land breeze at night (land → sea)
Valley breeze by day (upslope); mountain breeze at night (downslope)
Pressure belts: low at equator, high at ~30°, low at ~60°, high at poles
Coriolis effect: right in N hemisphere, left in S hemisphere
Gyres: large circular ocean currents
North Atlantic Drift keeps north-west Europe mild

topics.title: The water cycle and the carbon cycle
topics.summary: Water cycles through evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, runoff and infiltration, powered by the Sun. Carbon cycles fast (photosynthesis and respiration) and slowly (rocks and fossil fuels). Atmospheric CO₂ has risen from about 315 ppm in 1960 to over 420 ppm today.
topics.simple: The same water has been going round and round for billions of years: the Sun heats it, it **evaporates**, forms **clouds**, falls as **rain or snow**, and flows back to the sea. **Carbon** also moves around: plants take CO₂ from the air to make food, and living things breathe it back out. Some carbon gets locked up for millions of years in rocks and in coal and oil — and when we burn those, we release it quickly.
topics.explain:
**Water cycle** (powered by the Sun and gravity):
1. **Evaporation:** the Sun heats oceans, lakes and rivers; water becomes vapour.
2. **Transpiration:** plants release water vapour from their leaves.
3. **Condensation:** rising vapour cools and forms tiny droplets — **clouds**.
4. **Precipitation:** droplets grow and fall as rain, snow or hail.
5. **Runoff and infiltration:** water flows over land into rivers and seas, or soaks into the ground to become **groundwater**. Some is stored as ice in the cryosphere.

The water cycle links all five spheres and also moves heat: evaporation absorbs heat, and condensation releases it into the atmosphere.

**Carbon cycle** — carbon moves between air, living things, oceans and rocks.

**Fast carbon cycle** (days to years):
- **Photosynthesis:** plants and algae take in CO₂ to make food
- **Respiration:** plants, animals and microbes release CO₂
- **Decomposition:** decomposers break down dead matter, releasing CO₂
- **Oceans** dissolve and release CO₂

**Slow carbon cycle** (thousands to millions of years):
- Carbon gets stored in **rocks** like limestone (from shells and skeletons of sea creatures) and in **fossil fuels** — coal, petroleum and natural gas, formed from buried remains of ancient organisms
- It returns naturally through volcanoes and weathering of rocks

**Human effect:** burning fossil fuels and cutting forests release carbon much faster than nature can absorb it. Atmospheric CO₂ has risen from about **315 ppm (parts per million) around 1960** to **over 420 ppm today** — and pre-industrial levels were about 280 ppm.
topics.example: Worked example: CO₂ rose from about 315 ppm (1960) to about 420 ppm. Increase = 420 − 315 = 105 ppm. Percentage increase = (105 ÷ 315) × 100 ≈ **33%** — a one-third rise in about 65 years.
keyPoints: Water cycle: evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, runoff, infiltration
The Sun powers the water cycle
Fast carbon cycle: photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition
Slow carbon cycle: limestone rocks, fossil fuels, volcanoes
CO₂: ~315 ppm (1960) → over 420 ppm today
Burning fossil fuels releases long-stored carbon quickly

topics.title: The nitrogen cycle and the oxygen cycle
topics.summary: Nitrogen gas is fixed by lightning, Rhizobium in legume root nodules, Azotobacter and the Haber–Bosch process; then nitrification, assimilation, ammonification and denitrification complete the cycle. Oxygen is released by photosynthesis (6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂) and used in respiration and burning.
topics.simple: Nitrogen makes up 78% of air, but plants and animals can't use it directly. Lightning and special bacteria turn it into forms plants can absorb — some bacteria live in little lumps on the roots of pea and bean plants. Other bacteria later return nitrogen to the air. **Oxygen** is given out by plants during photosynthesis and used up when living things breathe and when things burn.
topics.explain:
**Why nitrogen matters:** it is needed to make **proteins** and **DNA**. But N₂ gas is very unreactive, so most organisms cannot use it directly.

**Nitrogen cycle — main steps:**
1. **Nitrogen fixation** — N₂ is changed into usable compounds (ammonia/nitrates):
   - **Lightning:** its energy makes nitrogen react with oxygen; the compounds dissolve in rain and reach the soil as nitrates.
   - **Rhizobium:** bacteria living in the **root nodules of legumes** (pea, gram, beans, groundnut). That's why farmers grow pulses to enrich soil.
   - **Azotobacter:** free-living bacteria in the soil (some cyanobacteria also fix nitrogen).
   - **Haber–Bosch process:** industry combines nitrogen and hydrogen to make **ammonia** for **fertilisers** (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃).
2. **Nitrification:** soil bacteria convert ammonia into **nitrites** and then **nitrates**.
3. **Assimilation:** plants absorb nitrates through their roots and build proteins; animals get nitrogen by eating plants or other animals.
4. **Ammonification:** when organisms die or excrete wastes, **decomposers** convert the nitrogen compounds back into **ammonia**.
5. **Denitrification:** other bacteria (especially in waterlogged soil) convert nitrates back into **N₂ gas**, returning it to the air.

**Oxygen cycle:**
- **Released** by **photosynthesis** in plants, algae and cyanobacteria (ocean phytoplankton produce a large share of Earth's oxygen):
  **6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂** (in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll)
- **Used** in **respiration** (by almost all living things), **combustion** (burning fuels) and **decomposition**; also in **rusting** and weathering of rocks
- In the stratosphere some oxygen forms **ozone (O₃)**

Photosynthesis and respiration are roughly reverse processes, which is why the carbon and oxygen cycles are closely linked.
topics.example: Farmers in India often grow a pulse crop like moong or chana between cereal crops. Rhizobium in the pulse roots fixes nitrogen, so the next crop of wheat or rice needs less chemical fertiliser — this is crop rotation.
keyPoints: N₂ (78% of air) can't be used directly by most organisms
Fixation: lightning, Rhizobium (legume root nodules), Azotobacter, Haber–Bosch
Nitrification: ammonia → nitrites → nitrates
Assimilation (plants absorb nitrates) → ammonification (decomposers) → denitrification (back to N₂)
Photosynthesis: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (sunlight, chlorophyll)
Oxygen used by respiration, combustion, decomposition

topics.title: Human impact and solutions
topics.summary: Humans are disturbing Earth's systems: global warming from greenhouse gases, eutrophication from fertiliser runoff, deforestation, ozone-layer depletion by CFCs and harmful ground-level ozone. Solutions include the Montreal Protocol (1987), the Paris Agreement (2015) and India's Mission LiFE.
topics.simple: Burning coal, oil and gas adds extra carbon dioxide to the air, which traps more heat — **global warming**. Too much fertiliser washing into lakes makes algae grow wildly and fish die. Cutting forests, and chemicals called **CFCs** that damage the ozone layer, cause harm too. But countries have worked together to fix problems — the world banned CFCs and the ozone layer is healing — and each of us can help through simple lifestyle choices.
topics.explain:
**1. Global warming and climate change:** greenhouse gases (CO₂, methane, nitrous oxide, water vapour) trap heat radiated by Earth. The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth habitable, but extra gases from burning **fossil fuels**, deforestation and farming have warmed Earth by **more than 1 °C** since pre-industrial times. Effects: melting glaciers and ice sheets, rising sea level, more heatwaves, floods and droughts.

**2. Eutrophication:** excess **fertilisers** (nitrates and phosphates) and sewage wash into lakes and rivers → **algae grow rapidly (algal bloom)** → when they die, decomposers use up the dissolved **oxygen** → fish and other animals die.

**3. Deforestation:** fewer trees to absorb CO₂; burning or rotting wood releases carbon; soil erosion; less rainfall from transpiration; loss of habitats and biodiversity.

**4. Ozone depletion:** **CFCs** (chlorofluorocarbons), once used in refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol sprays, rise to the stratosphere, where sunlight breaks them apart and the chlorine released destroys ozone. This created the **ozone hole** over Antarctica, letting in more UV rays that can cause skin cancer, cataracts and harm crops.

**5. Ground-level ozone:** near the ground, ozone is a harmful **pollutant**. It forms when pollutants from vehicles and industries react in sunlight, forming **smog**, which damages lungs and crops. Ozone is 'good up high, bad nearby'.

**Solutions:**
- **Montreal Protocol (1987):** countries agreed to phase out CFCs and other ozone-depleting substances. It worked — the ozone layer is slowly recovering. It is often called the most successful environmental treaty.
- **Paris Agreement (2015):** nearly all countries agreed to limit global warming to **well below 2 °C**, and try for **1.5 °C**, by cutting greenhouse gas emissions.
- **Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment):** an initiative led by **India** encouraging individuals to adopt eco-friendly habits — saving energy and water, reducing single-use plastic, cutting food waste, using public transport or cycling.
- Others: renewable energy (solar, wind), planting trees, careful use of fertilisers, cleaner fuels and vehicles.
topics.example: A green layer of algae spreading over a lake next to farm fields, followed by dead fish floating on the surface, is a classic sign of eutrophication caused by fertiliser runoff.
keyPoints: Greenhouse gases from fossil fuels → global warming (>1 °C so far)
Eutrophication: fertiliser runoff → algal bloom → oxygen loss → fish die
Deforestation reduces CO₂ absorption and causes erosion and habitat loss
CFCs destroy stratospheric ozone → ozone hole; more UV
Ground-level ozone is a harmful smog pollutant
Montreal Protocol (1987): CFCs phased out; Paris Agreement (2015): well below 2 °C, aim 1.5 °C
Mission LiFE (India): Lifestyle for Environment

faqs.q: What is the difference between the ozone hole and global warming?
faqs.a: The **ozone hole** is thinning of the ozone layer in the stratosphere caused mainly by **CFCs**; it lets more harmful **UV rays** reach the ground. **Global warming** is the rise in Earth's average temperature caused by extra **greenhouse gases** like CO₂ trapping heat. They are different problems with different causes and different treaties (Montreal Protocol vs Paris Agreement).

faqs.q: Why does a sea breeze blow during the day?
faqs.a: Land heats up faster than water. By day, the air over land becomes warmer, rises and leaves **low pressure**. Cooler air over the sea is at **higher pressure**, so it flows towards the land. At night land cools faster, so the direction reverses (land breeze).

faqs.q: Why is the equator hotter than the poles?
faqs.a: At the equator the Sun's rays strike almost **vertically**, so the energy is concentrated on a small area and passes through less atmosphere. At the poles the rays arrive at a **slant**, spreading the same energy over a larger area and passing through more air. Snow and ice at the poles also have a high albedo and reflect much of the sunlight.

faqs.q: If air is 78% nitrogen, why do plants need nitrogen fertiliser?
faqs.a: Nitrogen gas (N₂) is very unreactive, and plants cannot absorb it directly. They need nitrogen as **nitrates** or ammonium from the soil. Only fixation — by lightning, bacteria like Rhizobium and Azotobacter, or the Haber–Bosch process — converts N₂ into these usable forms.

Both, depending on where it is. **Stratospheric ozone** (12–50 km up) is good: it absorbs harmful UV radiation. **Ground-level ozone**, formed when vehicle and industrial pollutants react in sunlight, is bad: it is part of smog and damages lungs and crops.

faqs.q: What is albedo and why does melting ice make warming worse?
faqs.a: **Albedo** is the fraction of sunlight a surface reflects. Fresh snow reflects about 80–90%, while ocean water reflects only about 6–10%. When ice melts, darker water or land underneath absorbs more sunlight, heats up more, and melts even more ice — a feedback that speeds up warming.
